issues.subcategory: contradictory operationalization of moral incongruence
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly defines moral incongruence as the interaction between moral disapproval and behavioral frequency, but later states that it will be measured as an interaction with severity of consequences. These are substantively different constructs: frequency captures exposure/engagement, whereas consequences overlap with the outcome/problem severity. This contradiction makes the primary hypothesis and model specification unclear and could produce circular prediction if consequences are used as a predictor of problematic use.
issues.quote: Central to the proposed study is the measurement of moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action.

issues.subcategory: equivalence interval contradiction
issues.description: The analytic plan specifies two different smallest effects/equivalence bounds: δ = .27 and δ = |.11|. These would lead to different conclusions about whether an effect is practically null. The contradiction is critical because equivalence testing is central to the hypotheses that moral incongruence is absent for gambling and substances.
issues.quote: We will use the Anderson-Hauck equivalence test for regression (Counsell & Cribbie, 2015), with an equivalence region based on the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) of δ= .27. ... setting our equivalence region to δ= |.11| represents an extremely conservative analytic decision.

issues.subcategory: inconsistent frequency coding and skip criterion
issues.description: Pornography frequency is described as ranging from 1 to 6 in the methods, while the supplemental materials use 0 to 5. The stated skip criterion of scores > 1 has different meanings under these codings and could either include or exclude participants who used pornography once or twice. This affects analytic inclusion, sample size, and interpretation of frequency effects.
issues.quote: Pornography viewing frequency will be assessed using the same modified frequency scale as is present on the ASSIST, wherein participants will report past-year frequency of pornography use on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day). Like the above-described process for the ASSIST, only participants who report viewing pornography at least once in the past 12 months (i.e., scores > 1 on the frequency measure) will complete the remaining items described below.

issues.subcategory: Brief Pornography Screen scoring inconsistency
issues.description: The methods state that BPS items are scored 0 to 2, but the supplemental materials show response values of 0, 2, and 4. This changes the possible total score, scale variance, standardized effects, and any interpretation of symptom severity.
issues.quote: Participants will respond to the prompt, “In the last 6 months, have any of these situations happened to you in regards to your use of pornography?” by reporting the frequency they have experienced certain behaviors ... on a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often). Responses are summed. ... Brief Pornography Screen ... Never (0) | Occasionally (2) | Very Often (4)

issues.subcategory: Problem Gambling Severity Index scoring inconsistency
issues.description: The methods describe PGSI scoring as 0 to 3, whereas the supplemental response options are scored 0, 2, 4, and 5. This is also not the standard PGSI scoring of 0, 1, 2, 3. The inconsistency threatens reproducibility and invalidates comparisons to validated PGSI thresholds or prior literature.
issues.quote: This 9-item measure requires participants to respond to a series of questions ... on a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always). Responses will be averaged. ... Never (0) | Sometimes (2) | Most of the time (4) | Almost Always (5)

issues.subcategory: contradictory skip logic and analytic inclusion
issues.description: The measures section says only participants endorsing past-year use will complete problematic-use measures, but the data-screening section says problematic-use and moral-disapproval measures will be administered to all participants regardless of engagement. This affects missingness, denominator definitions, whether non-users are modeled as zeros or excluded, and the interpretation of moral incongruence.
issues.quote: Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use. ... For each target behavior and corresponding measure of problematic use or addiction, key measures will be administered to all participants regardless of their engagement in the behavior. That is, we will administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to all participants in the sample.

issues.subcategory: gambling frequency measure described inconsistently
issues.description: The manuscript says gambling frequency will be assessed with a single item, then says an average across gambling behaviors will be taken. The supplemental materials show only one global gambling item. It is therefore unclear what variable will be analyzed and how gambling frequency will be computed.
issues.quote: We will assess gambling frequency using a single item. ... To form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken.

issues.subcategory: number of outcomes and moderation analyses unclear
issues.description: The analytic plan alternates between eight proposed outcomes, eight moderation analyses, and tables that include seven domains with additional modified NIDA-ASSIST outcomes for pornography and gambling. This makes the primary confirmatory tests ambiguous and creates room for selective reporting.
issues.quote: Prior to our primary analyses, assumptions of regression ... will be tested for each of the eight proposed outcomes. ... In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest, with pornography and gambling assessed using the validate measures of problematic use ... Table 1 ... Pornography Use | Brief Pornography Screen Sum Score and modified NIDA-ASSIST items; Gambling Behavior | Problem Gambling Severity Index and modified NIDA-ASSIST items

issues.subcategory: nicotine variables described inconsistently
issues.description: The methods refer to tobacco and non-tobacco nicotine as separate substances when describing outcome scores, but the actual measure appears to use a single combined tobacco/nicotine item. This ambiguity affects the number of analyzed domains and the construction of substance-specific outcomes.
issues.quote: Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged for each substance of interest (i.e., alcohol, tobacco, non-tobacco nicotine, prescription drugs, illicit drugs, cannabis).

issues.subcategory: male alcohol item label inconsistent with prompt
issues.description: The supplemental materials say men are asked about more than 5 drinks, but the response row is labeled “More than four drinks.” This could confuse respondents or indicate a programming/scoring error for the alcohol quantity item.
issues.quote: IF GENDER = MAN In the past year, how often have you had more than 5 drinks on one occasion? ... More than four drinks (1)

issues.subcategory: unweighted analysis despite matched sample and oversample
issues.description: The study plans ordinary regression using lm but does not mention survey weights, post-stratification weights, design variables, or adjustment for the sports-wagering oversample. Pooling a representative sample with a purposive sports-wagering oversample without weights or design indicators will bias population estimates and regression associations, especially for gambling and correlated substance-use outcomes.
issues.quote: This will provide us with a total sample of over 4,000 American adults. ... As a primary test of our key hypotheses, we will conduct moderation analyses using the lm function in the stats package for R statistical software

issues.subcategory: OLS model inappropriate or underspecified for bounded ordinal zero-inflated outcomes
issues.description: The planned OLS models treat ordinal frequency predictors, single-item ordinal moral-disapproval measures, and bounded symptom scales as continuous and normally distributed. BPS, PGSI, and ASSIST averages are likely skewed and zero-inflated, especially among community samples and low-prevalence drug users. The manuscript only vaguely promises supplemental analyses if assumptions are violated, without prespecifying robust, ordinal, count, zero-inflated, or generalized models.
issues.quote: As a primary test of our key hypotheses, we will conduct moderation analyses using the lm function in the stats package for R statistical software ... Prior to our primary analyses, assumptions of regression ... will be tested for each of the eight proposed outcomes.

issues.subcategory: power analysis targets detection not equivalence
issues.description: The power analysis focuses on detecting an effect of f2 = .015 using G*Power. However, the key null hypotheses require sufficient precision to conclude equivalence, which requires equivalence-test-specific power based on the expected standard error and equivalence bounds. Power to reject a null effect is not the same as power to conclude practical equivalence.
issues.quote: we conducted a power analysis to determine the sample size needed to reliably detect our smallest effect of interest (f2 = .015), a series of sensitivity analyses to determine the likely power our final sample sizes would have to detect the effect size associated with our SESOI and equivalence region defined above

issues.subcategory: adaptive post hoc equivalence bound
issues.description: The plan allows the equivalence region to be redefined after seeing the pornography result or when underpowered. This changes the hypothesis from equivalence to zero into equivalence relative to an observed benchmark and can bias conclusions. A confirmatory registered report should prespecify a single primary SESOI or direct comparative test.
issues.quote: In the event that, contrary to hypotheses, the effects of moral incongruence for gambling and substances exceed our region of equivalence based on our SESOI, we will conduct exploratory analyses wherein we redefine the region of equivalence using the lower bounds of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate for our pornography outcome.

issues.subcategory: standardized interaction coefficients not comparable across heterogeneous outcomes
issues.description: The study proposes comparing standardized interaction coefficients across pornography, gambling, and substances. Standardized product-term coefficients depend on the variances, reliabilities, distributions, and range restrictions of both predictors and outcomes. Because the domains use different scales, base rates, and measurement reliability, the same standardized beta does not represent the same substantive effect across domains.
issues.quote: Should the confidence interval for the observed standardized effect of the interaction for moral disapproval of a behavior and frequency of that behavior fall fully within our equivalence region, we may reasonably conclude that the true effect is so low as to be null or practically null

issues.subcategory: no direct statistical test of cross-domain differences
issues.description: The central claim concerns whether moral incongruence is unique to pornography/sexual behavior, but the plan relies on whether separate coefficients are significant or equivalent. It does not specify a direct test comparing interaction coefficients across domains, accounting for within-person dependence and different measurement error. Separate significance/equivalence decisions cannot establish that effects differ between domains.
issues.quote: should we find that moral incongruence—defined as the interaction between moral disapproval of a behavior and the frequency of engaging in that behavior—only predicts self-reported problematic use of pornography, then this work would provide strong evidence for the validity of the PPMI as a unique model

issues.subcategory: primary multiple testing not controlled
issues.description: The study will conduct many moderation tests across behaviors and outcomes, but no multiplicity correction or hierarchical testing plan is specified for the primary hypotheses. This increases the risk of false positives and selective emphasis, especially because the confirmatory conclusions depend on domain-specific patterns of significance and equivalence.
issues.quote: In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest

issues.subcategory: incorrect phrasing about Holm-adjusted statistics
issues.description: The manuscript states that bivariate correlations will use Holm-adjusted test statistics. Holm adjustment applies to p-values or significance thresholds, not the correlation test statistics themselves. This is a minor but concrete statistical reporting error.
issues.quote: Bivariate correlations will be conducted across all included measures and reported using Holm-adjusted test statistics using the psych package.

issues.subcategory: vague unspecified robustness analyses
issues.description: The analytic plan leaves major decisions to be made after inspecting assumption violations, using phrases such as “substantially violated” and “as appropriate.” It does not define diagnostic thresholds or the alternative models to be used. This undermines the confirmatory value of the registered report.
issues.quote: in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate.

issues.subcategory: inconsistent centering and product-term construction
issues.description: The manuscript first says focal predictors and moderators will be centered before computing the interaction, then later says key variables will be entered in raw form and their product computed. Centering affects lower-order coefficients and, for standardized interaction terms, can affect interpretation and comparability. The preprocessing plan is not reproducible.
issues.quote: focal predictors (behavioral frequency measures) and moderators (moral disapproval questions) will be centered and their interaction term calculated. ... For moderation analyses, key variables will be entered in their raw form during data processing in SPSS, and their product will be computed.

issues.subcategory: unclear primary outcome hierarchy
issues.description: Pornography and gambling are assessed using both validated scales and modified NIDA-ASSIST items, but the primary outcome for each hypothesis is not consistently specified. The plan also proposes using the pornography NIDA-ASSIST interaction to set later equivalence bounds, even though the main pornography hypothesis appears to emphasize the BPS. This creates researcher degrees of freedom.
issues.quote: Pornography Use | Brief Pornography Screen Sum Score and modified NIDA-ASSIST items ... Gambling Behavior | Problem Gambling Severity Index and modified NIDA-ASSIST items ... Specifically, we will use the lower limit of the 95% confidence interval around the obtained standardized estimate for the effect of the interaction of moral disapproval and pornography viewing frequency in predicting self-reported feelings of addiction to pornography using the modified NIDA-ASSIST items for pornography.

issues.subcategory: no clear stopping rule or quota failure plan
issues.description: The manuscript gives target sample sizes but does not specify stopping rules, whether data collection may exceed or fall short of targets, how quota failures will be handled, or whether analyses will proceed if the national and oversample components differ from plan. This is important for a registered report using panel recruitment.
issues.quote: the target sample size will be 2,500 American adults that match nationally representative norms for age and gender. Furthermore ... we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports

issues.subcategory: representative sample combined with nonrepresentative oversample
issues.description: The study describes a representative U.S. sample plus an additional sports-wagering oversample, then refers to the total as a study of the American public. Unless weighted or analyzed separately, the combined sample is not population representative. This is especially problematic because sports wagering is likely associated with gambling severity, substance use, demographics, and moral attitudes.
issues.quote: the target sample size will be 2,500 American adults that match nationally representative norms for age and gender. Furthermore ... we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically. This will provide us with a total sample of over 4,000 American adults.

issues.subcategory: limited matching variables for representativeness
issues.description: The manuscript claims national representativeness, but matching is described only for age and gender. Moral disapproval, pornography use, gambling, and substance use vary by race/ethnicity, education, income, region, religion, political ideology, and state policy context. Age/gender matching alone is insufficient for representative inference.
issues.quote: matched to U.S. representative norms. ... the target sample size will be 2,500 American adults that match nationally representative norms for age and gender.

issues.subcategory: careless responding controls delegated to proprietary vendor
issues.description: The study states that no exclusions for inattentive or invalid responses are anticipated because YouGov has proprietary quality-control procedures. Without reporting the actual checks, thresholds, exclusions, or response-time rules, readers cannot evaluate data quality or reproduce the screening process.
issues.quote: certain measures of quality control and responsiveness are guaranteed as a part of their data collection process based on their proprietary data collection standards. Accordingly, we do not anticipate having to remove responses from the dataset due to inattentive or invalid response styles or due to careless responding.

issues.subcategory: binary gender coding collapses heterogeneous groups
issues.description: The analytic plan codes gender as male versus not-male, collapsing women with nonbinary or other gender identities. This may obscure meaningful differences and creates ambiguity for gender-specific alcohol items. The plan does not state how nonbinary, missing, or “prefer not to say” responses will be handled.
issues.quote: Interactions will be tested using this program with gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male), age, and overall religiousness included as covariates of the outcome.

issues.subcategory: no control for state legality or policy context
issues.description: Cannabis legality and sports-betting legality vary substantially by state, and these contexts can affect both behavior frequency and whether respondents view the behavior as morally wrong or problematic. State is available from YouGov but not included as a covariate or stratification factor.
issues.quote: State of Residence ... Region ... We intend on including religiousness, age, and gender as covariates

issues.subcategory: survey timing may bias gambling behavior
issues.description: Recruitment is planned for late March, during a period with unusually salient U.S. sports wagering opportunities. This may inflate recent gambling salience or reporting, particularly in a sports-wagering oversample, but no seasonal limitation or control is specified.
issues.quote: Participants will be recruited in late March of 2022 as a part of a larger study of sports wagering behaviors

issues.subcategory: moral disapproval is not moral distress
issues.description: The theoretical and diagnostic rationale concerns moral distress, but the study measures only agreement that a behavior is morally wrong. Disapproval and distress are not equivalent; a person may disapprove without distress or feel distress without endorsing a simple moral-wrongness item. This weakens conclusions about the ICD-11 moral-distress caveat.
issues.quote: distress related to moral disapproval of one’s own sexual behaviors is not sufficient to receive the diagnosis. ... we will ask participants to rate their agreement with the following statement “I believe that using ________ is morally wrong”

issues.subcategory: single-item moral-disapproval measures
issues.description: Moral disapproval is central to every model but is measured with one item per domain. Single items provide no estimate of reliability, may be interpreted differently across behaviors, and cannot distinguish religious morality, legality, harm concerns, disgust, stigma, or personal values. Measurement error can attenuate interactions and bias equivalence conclusions.
issues.quote: Additionally, we will include a series of single-item moral disapproval questions that match previous measures of moral disapproval of pornography.

issues.subcategory: generic moral item does not assess incongruence with own behavior
issues.description: The moral items ask whether the behavior is morally wrong in general, not whether the respondent’s own behavior violates their values or causes self-evaluative conflict. This is a mismatch with the construct of moral incongruence, which requires a discrepancy between personal values and one’s own behavior.
issues.quote: Participants will respond on a scale of 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree) to the prompt: “I believe that gambling is morally wrong.”

issues.subcategory: statistical interaction does not directly measure value-behavior discrepancy
issues.description: The manuscript equates moral incongruence with a product term between disapproval and frequency. A product term tests moderation, not necessarily subjective incongruence, conflict, guilt, shame, or distress about violating values. Individuals high in disapproval and low in use, or moderate in both, may not fit the conceptual construct implied by the theory.
issues.quote: moral incongruence (defined as the interaction of moral disapproval of a behavior and the frequency of engaging in that behavior)

issues.subcategory: outcome measures contain moral/guilt content
issues.description: The key outcomes include guilt items, which overlap directly with moral disapproval and moral distress. This criterion contamination can inflate associations between moral disapproval and “addiction” scores and makes it difficult to distinguish perceived dysregulation from moralized self-evaluation.
issues.quote: You continue to use pornography even though you feel guilty about it. ... Have you felt guilty about the way you gamble or what happens when you gamble?

issues.subcategory: modified NIDA-ASSIST not validated for pornography or gambling
issues.description: The study adds pornography and gambling to the NIDA-ASSIST despite acknowledging the approach is not validated. The ASSIST was designed for substance involvement, and its items may not have the same structure, severity meaning, or psychometric validity for behaviors such as pornography viewing or gambling.
issues.quote: We will also include pornography and gambling as response options on the NIDA-ASSIST ... Although such an approach is not currently validated for gambling or pornography

issues.subcategory: ASSIST modifications undermine validated scoring
issues.description: The study substantially modifies the ASSIST/Quick Screen and then averages items, rather than using validated ASSIST scoring. Items use different response ranges and time frames, and the two lifetime/past-three-month items are scored 0/3/6 while other items are 0–5. Averaging them imposes arbitrary weights and may not represent substance-use-disorder severity.
issues.quote: To assess problematic or potentially addictive use of these substances, we will take the average of responses to problematic use questions present in the NIDA-ASSIST. ... Participants will respond to three frequency based questions ... on a scale of 0 (never) to 5 (more than once per day) ... Participants will also respond to two questions ... on 3 point scale (0 = No, Never; 3 = Yes, but not in the past 3 months; and 6 = Yes, In the past 3 months). Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged

issues.subcategory: outcome does not directly measure self-perceived addiction across domains
issues.description: The stated construct is self-reported feelings of addiction, but the proposed outcomes are screening/symptom scales for pornography, gambling, and substance problems. These are not equivalent to self-identifying as addicted, and the construct differs from the prior literature the manuscript seeks to extend.
issues.quote: self-perceived feelings of addiction to both behaviors ... and substances ... Problem gambling behavior will be measured using the Problem Gambling Severity Index ... To assess problematic or potentially addictive use of these substances, we will take the average of responses to problematic use questions present in the NIDA-ASSIST.

issues.subcategory: time-frame mismatch among predictor, moderator, and outcomes
issues.description: The planned models combine past-year behavioral frequency, current moral disapproval, past-three-month ASSIST symptoms, lifetime/past-three-month ASSIST items, six-month BPS symptoms, and twelve-month PGSI symptoms. These mismatched time frames weaken temporal and construct alignment and can obscure or create interactions.
issues.quote: In its original form, the NIDA Quick Screen provides a response range ... participants will report the frequency with which they have engaged in those behaviors over the past 12 months ... Participants will respond to three frequency based questions ... In the past three months ... Participants will respond to the prompt, “In the last 6 months...” ... Problem Gambling Severity Index Thinking about the last 12 months

issues.subcategory: behavior frequency is an inadequate exposure measure
issues.description: Frequency alone does not capture quantity, intensity, dose, money lost, intoxication, potency, duration, or binge patterns. For alcohol, drugs, gambling, and pornography, these dimensions are often more relevant to problematic use than frequency. This weakens cross-domain comparisons and may bias interactions differently by behavior.
issues.quote: we will look at alcohol frequency more generally (i.e., asking participants how often they have consumed alcohol without specifying the quantity consumed).

issues.subcategory: frequency scale not comparable across behaviors
issues.description: The same ordinal frequency categories are used for behaviors with very different natural units. “More than once per day” has different meanings for nicotine, alcohol, lottery purchases, pornography, and illicit drugs. Treating these scales as comparable continuous predictors makes cross-domain standardized interaction comparisons conceptually weak.
issues.quote: we will modify response options by adding an additional frequency category of more than once per day so that participants will report the frequency with which they have engaged in those behaviors over the past 12 months on a scale of 0 (never) to 5 (more than once per day).

issues.subcategory: pornography frequency excludes partnered use
issues.description: The supplemental frequency item assesses viewing pornography alone, whereas moral disapproval and BPS items refer to pornography use generally. Participants who use pornography with partners may be misclassified or have mismatched predictor and outcome responses.
issues.quote: Viewed pornography alone (i.e., without a partner) ... I believe that pornography use is morally wrong.

issues.subcategory: gambling construct too heterogeneous for one moral item
issues.description: The gambling frequency item combines lotteries, casino gambling, fantasy sports, esports betting, online betting, and card games. Moral attitudes and risk profiles may differ sharply across these activities. A single global frequency and single global moral-disapproval item may not correspond to the specific gambling behavior causing problems.
issues.quote: Examples of these types of activities include: gambling in casinos or online, buying lottery tickets, playing fantasy sports for money, placing bets on esports, placing bets on traditional sporting events, playing cards for money, placing bets online.

issues.subcategory: substance categories confound morality with legality and harm
issues.description: Items for illegal drugs and nonmedical prescription drug use embed legal or misuse status in the construct. Endorsing that “illegal/illicit drugs” or “prescription drugs for non-medical reasons” are morally wrong may reflect legality, perceived dangerousness, or social desirability rather than personal moral incongruence. Restricted variance or ceiling effects could produce false equivalence.
issues.quote: I believe that using prescription drugs for non-medical reasons is morally wrong ... I believe that using illegal/illicit drugs is morally wrong.

issues.subcategory: substance-use-disorder symptoms incompletely measured
issues.description: The modified ASSIST items do not assess the full DSM/ICD substance-use-disorder symptom set, including tolerance, withdrawal, hazardous use, longer/larger use than intended, or time spent obtaining/using/recovering. Therefore, conclusions about substance use disorders are not supported by the proposed measures.
issues.quote: Participants will respond to three frequency based questions that assess problematic use ... Participants will also respond to two questions ... Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged for each substance of interest

issues.subcategory: cross-sectional design but causal language
issues.description: The study is cross-sectional, but the manuscript uses causal language such as moral incongruence “influences” feelings of addiction and “contributor.” Without temporal ordering or experimental manipulation, associations cannot establish that moral disapproval or incongruence causes perceived addiction or symptoms.
issues.quote: we seek to establish whether moral incongruence ... influences self-perceived feelings of addiction ... This sample is cross-sectional, which limits the temporal ordering of variables.

issues.subcategory: limited confounder adjustment
issues.description: The planned covariates are age, gender, and religiousness only. Many plausible confounders are available or relevant, including race/ethnicity, education, income, marital status, political ideology, region, state legality, mental health, treatment history, social desirability, and severity/quantity of behavior. Unadjusted confounding may explain associations between moral disapproval, behavior frequency, and self-reported problems.
issues.quote: In each case, we intend on including religiousness, age, and gender as covariates

issues.subcategory: no basis for distinguishing false positives from true dysregulation
issues.description: The manuscript suggests that moral incongruence may create false-positive diagnoses, but the study has no clinical interview, clinician-rated impairment, collateral report, or objective behavioral indicators sufficient to distinguish moral distress from actual dysregulation. Self-report symptom scales alone cannot validate diagnostic false positives.
issues.quote: the real potential concern associated with this effect is whether it creates false-positive diagnoses in clinical settings.

issues.subcategory: family concern outcome may reflect others' morality
issues.description: One ASSIST outcome item asks whether others expressed concern. For behaviors such as pornography, gambling, alcohol, cannabis, or illicit drugs, others’ concern may reflect family or community moral norms rather than impairment. This creates confounding between moral context and the outcome labeled as addiction/problem severity.
issues.quote: Has a friend or relative or anyone else ever expressed concern about your use of or engagement in the following?

issues.subcategory: missing survey weights and sampling details
issues.description: The manuscript does not report how YouGov matching will be performed, whether survey weights will be supplied, which benchmarks will be used, or how the sports-wagering oversample will be incorporated. Without these details, the representativeness and replicability of the analyses cannot be evaluated.
issues.quote: Participants will be recruited by YouGov Opinion Polling and matched to U.S. representative norms.

issues.subcategory: missing recruitment and response-rate information
issues.description: The methods omit important panel-survey details: sampling frame, invitation procedures, eligibility screening, response rate, completion rate, compensation, device/mode, and whether respondents can skip sensitive items. These details are needed to assess selection bias and replicate the study.
issues.quote: Participants will be recruited by YouGov Opinion Polling and matched to U.S. representative norms.

issues.subcategory: missing ethics and consent information
issues.description: The manuscript does not mention IRB/ethics approval, informed consent, privacy protections, or risk mitigation for sensitive questions about pornography, illicit drug use, and gambling. This is a reporting gap for human-subjects research.
issues.quote: Participants will be recruited in late March of 2022 as a part of a larger study of sports wagering behaviors in the American populace funded by the International Center for Responsible Gaming.

issues.subcategory: proprietary quality control not auditable
issues.description: The paper relies on unspecified proprietary data-quality procedures. Readers cannot evaluate attention checks, duplicate prevention, bot detection, speeding thresholds, or exclusion rates, and these procedures cannot be reproduced by independent researchers.
issues.quote: based on their proprietary data collection standards

issues.subcategory: conflict-of-interest/funder role not described
issues.description: The study is funded by an organization focused on responsible gambling, but the manuscript does not describe the funder's role in study design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, or publication. Given the gambling focus and sports-wagering oversample, this information is important for evaluating potential bias.
issues.quote: funded by the International Center for Responsible Gaming

issues.subcategory: unrealistic no-missing-data assumption
issues.description: The manuscript assumes no unplanned missingness, despite sensitive survey content and use of panel data. It does not specify how missing panel covariates, skipped sensitive items, partial completions, refusals, or survey breakoffs will be handled. This threatens reproducibility and may bias analyses if missingness is related to morality or behavior.
issues.quote: Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data.

issues.subcategory: no plan for skip-induced missingness
issues.description: If only past-year users complete problematic-use measures, missingness is structurally induced for non-users. The manuscript does not specify whether non-users are excluded, coded zero, or handled differently across outcomes. This affects sample sizes, power, and the meaning of regression coefficients.
issues.quote: Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use.

issues.subcategory: no dropout or partial-completion handling plan
issues.description: The data-screening section discusses inattentive responding but not survey attrition, partial completions, or whether incomplete cases will be retained. Sensitive items about pornography and illicit drugs may produce item nonresponse or breakoff.
issues.quote: we do not anticipate having to remove responses from the dataset due to inattentive or invalid response styles or due to careless responding

issues.subcategory: overclaiming from U.S. sample to diagnostic nosology
issues.description: The study uses a U.S. online panel but proposes conclusions about ICD-11 diagnostic considerations. Moral norms, legality, stigma, pornography attitudes, gambling availability, and substance policies vary across cultures and clinical settings, so U.S. community-panel findings cannot strongly validate or invalidate international diagnostic caveats.
issues.quote: should hypotheses be confirmed, there would be additional evidence supporting the inclusion of moral distress as a diagnostic consideration in the ICD-11 for CSBD.

issues.subcategory: pornography not equivalent to CSBD or sexual behavior broadly
issues.description: The empirical test focuses primarily on pornography use, but the conclusions are framed as applying to sexual behavior and CSBD. CSBD can involve diverse behaviors, impairment patterns, and clinical presentations. Findings about pornography viewing in a community sample may not generalize to compulsive sexual behavior disorder.
issues.quote: the role moral incongruence in predicting feelings of dysregulation is unique to sexual behavior ... Interactions ... will be tested ... for pornography use

issues.subcategory: community sample cannot generalize to treatment-seeking populations
issues.description: The manuscript acknowledges that clinical false positives are the key concern but studies a population sample. Treatment-seeking individuals differ in severity, distress, impairment, comorbidity, and help-seeking motivations. Population associations cannot determine clinical diagnostic performance.
issues.quote: it is likely that the effects of moral incongruence on feelings of addiction are most critical in treatment seeking populations. Identifying the presence or the effect of moral incongruence in the general public is important, but the real potential concern associated with this effect is whether it creates false-positive diagnoses in clinical settings.

issues.subcategory: combined sample may overrepresent gamblers and related risk profiles
issues.description: The sports-wagering oversample changes the composition of the total sample and may overrepresent young men, higher-risk gamblers, substance users, and people in states with legal sports betting. Generalizing pooled results to the American public would be inappropriate without weighting or stratification.
issues.quote: we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically

issues.subcategory: absence of evidence interpreted as evidence of uniqueness
issues.description: The theoretical conclusion depends on finding an interaction for pornography but not for other domains. Even with equivalence tests, null or smaller effects in other domains could reflect poor measurement, restricted variance, low reliability, different base rates, or inadequate power rather than true theoretical uniqueness.
issues.quote: Demonstrating that moral incongruence appears to only be relevant in predicting feelings of dysregulation for sexual behaviors would corroborate the importance of CSBD being the only disorder to include a consideration about moral distress.

issues.subcategory: misalignment between CSBD moral caveat and measured predictor
issues.description: The ICD-11 caveat concerns distress entirely related to moral judgments being insufficient for diagnosis, but the study tests whether moral disapproval moderates frequency-symptom associations. This does not directly test whether distress is entirely moral, whether symptoms meet CSBD criteria, or whether moral distress should be diagnostically excluded.
issues.quote: Diagnostic criteria for Compulsive Sexual Behavior Disorder (CSBD) specifically note that moral distress related to sexual behavior is not sufficient to receive the diagnosis. ... moral incongruence (defined as the interaction of moral disapproval of a behavior and the frequency of engaging in that behavior)

issues.subcategory: recognized addiction comparisons are not parallel
issues.description: The manuscript compares pornography use with gambling and substances as recognized addictions, but the measurement and diagnostic status are not parallel. Pornography is not itself a recognized addiction diagnosis in ICD/DSM, gambling disorder is behavioral, and substances are grouped into broad heterogeneous categories. This weakens theoretical claims about uniqueness across addiction types.
issues.quote: We propose to test these associations for pornography use and recognized addictive disorders such as gambling and substance use disorders (i.e., alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, illicit substances, and prescription drug misuse)

issues.subcategory: moral disapproval may be consequence rather than antecedent
issues.description: The model assumes moral disapproval contributes to perceived addiction, but people may increase moral disapproval after experiencing harms, failed control, or social consequences. The cross-sectional design cannot distinguish moral disapproval as a cause, correlate, or consequence of problematic behavior.
issues.quote: we expect to find that the simple, direct effect of moral disapproval of pornography on self-reported feelings of addiction to pornography will be significant and positive
